column6: The commentary's day makes every act answerable through a written record; Daniel's Aramaic vision seats the court before the Ancient of Days and opens books. It supplies the same concentrated scene of final judicial authority and record.

The commentary develops Arabic dîn as judgment, account, and recompense; Daniel calls the seated court dîn in Biblical Aramaic. The actual cognate is used there precisely for the court that opens the books.

The commentary says the deferred account arrives with a written book and exact repayment; Revelation has the dead stand before a throne, books open, and judgment proceed from what is written and done.
The commentary makes the day one on which no person's work escapes payment; Paul says all must appear before Christ's tribunal to receive for the things done in the body.
The commentary distinguishes a human court's limit from God's accounting for what is hidden within; Paul locates God's judgment specifically in the hidden things of people.
The commentary says the day exposes what written contracts and outward witnesses cannot reach; Paul says the Lord will bring hidden things to light and disclose the purposes of hearts.
The commentary joins the heart's concealed gain to final recompense; Jeremiah depicts YHWH as searching heart and mind in order to give each person according to conduct.
The commentary's final ledger includes what a person concealed; Qohelet says God brings every deed, including every hidden thing, into judgment.

column5: seeing eye; hearing ear; written book
column6: The commentary's record is not merely a human document but an exhaustive divine account; Avot turns that claim into an ethical warning through God's seeing, hearing, and the book in which all deeds are written.

column5: open ledger; credit; collectors; true judgment
column6: The commentary reads dîn through debt, a due date, writing, and full settlement; Akiva's saying imagines life as credit entered in an open ledger, collected without exception, ending in a true judgment.

column5: account and reckoning before King of kings
column6: The commentary calls the owner of the day the sole ruler before whom people stand; Avot frames mortal life as preparation to give account and reckoning before the King of kings.
The commentary emphasizes differentiated repayment from a preserved record; this talmudic discussion opens books for the wholly righteous, wholly wicked, and intermediates on the day of judgment.
The commentary's owner of the day presides over a universal judicial scene; Enoch presents the Head of Days seated on a throne while the books of the living are opened before the heavenly host.
The commentary links remembered deeds, a book, and the approaching day; Malachi records a book of remembrance before YHWH for those who fear him as it moves toward the day when he acts.

column5: book and deliverance at final time
column6: The commentary has people individually counted and brought to the day; Daniel's time of unparalleled trouble delivers those found written in the book.
The commentary treats the day as the event in which final recompense arrives; Daniel's sleepers awake to two sharply different enduring outcomes.
The commentary's day brings people out for a decisive accounting; John describes those in the tombs coming out into resurrection of life or resurrection of judgment.
The commentary places the day amid the trumpet and an altered created order; Paul makes the last trumpet the moment when the dead are raised and the living changed.

column5: time to judge dead and reward servants
column6: The commentary's single day pays every person and exposes rival rule; Revelation's trumpet vision calls it the time to judge the dead, reward God's servants, and destroy destroyers of the earth.

The commentary presents the day as the direct exercise of its one owner's judgment; Paul also says God fixed a day for world judgment, but specifies that he will judge through a man appointed and validated by resurrection.

column5: all judgment given to the Son
column6: The commentary's claim that all lesser possession and authority fall away leaves one owner of judgment; John assigns all judgment from the Father to the Son, a specifically Christological distribution of that role.

column5: YHWH alone exalted in that day
column6: The commentary says the day leaves one answer to the question of rule; Isaiah's day humbles every human height so that YHWH alone is exalted.
The commentary insists that worldly possession and dominion are lent and can be withdrawn; Daniel's king is made to confess that the Most High rules human kingdoms and gives them to whom he wills.

column5: source m-l-k; Hebrew melek; judge and king
column6: The commentary distinguishes the Arabic m-l-k words for owner and king while joining authority and judgment; Isaiah names YHWH both judge and king, using Hebrew melek, a cognate of the commentary's malik/melik family.

column5: YHWH one king over all earth
column6: The commentary's day reduces contested dominion to one owner; Zechariah's eschatological vision makes YHWH king over all earth and stresses his oneness.

The commentary develops possession as a relation of master and servant, then makes all people arrive as servants; Leviticus grounds Israel's release from human bondage in their belonging as servants to YHWH.

column5: all lives belong to God; individual liability
column6: The commentary joins belonging to God with personal accounting; Ezekiel says every life belongs to God and immediately makes the sinner, rather than a relative, answer for sin.
The commentary says death cannot remove a person from the owner's claim; Paul says Christ died and lived again in order to be Lord of both the dead and the living.

column5: body not one's own; bought at a price
column6: The commentary's owner-servant language denies autonomous human possession; Paul tells believers that they are not their own because they were bought at a price.

column5: Noah, Daniel, Job save only themselves
column6: The commentary says neither a parent, child, friend, nor other human can pay for another on that day; Ezekiel says even three exemplary righteous figures would deliver only themselves amid judgment.
The commentary renders the collapse of family and patronage as each person's individual reckoning; Paul states that each of us will give an account of himself to God.

column5: silver and gold cannot deliver in YHWH's day
column6: The commentary contrasts what hands possess with what can actually save on the day; Zephaniah says neither silver nor gold can deliver its owner on YHWH's day of wrath.

column5: riches fail on day of wrath
column6: The commentary's mal and children lose their usefulness when the account comes due; Proverbs directly says riches do not profit in a day of wrath.
The commentary says a person cannot offer another person or any possession as final payment; Jesus asks what anyone could give in exchange for the life or soul.

The commentary portrays death as the moment human ownership proves powerless and the person comes alone; the rich fool hears that his life is demanded that night and his accumulated things will belong to someone else.

column5: source yawm; Hebrew yom; solar days
column6: The commentary first defines yawm by sunrise and sunset before showing that the judgment day breaks that measure; Genesis uses cognate Hebrew yom for days and years marked by the heavenly lights, establishing the ordinary solar frame.

column5: unique day, neither day nor night
column6: The commentary calls the judgment day a duration no longer measured by the sun; Zechariah describes a unique day known to YHWH that is neither ordinary day nor night.
The commentary deliberately detaches the final day from human solar duration; 2 Peter likewise measures a day and a thousand years differently before describing the day of the Lord.
The commentary's day outlasts the solar clock because the heavenly lights themselves are undone; Isaiah's day of wrath darkens the stars, sun, and moon.
The commentary imagines the day after the sun's ordinary measuring work has ceased; Jesus' eschatological discourse darkens sun and moon after tribulation.
The commentary speaks of the heavens being folded in the day of God's grasp; Isaiah depicts the host of heaven decaying and the skies rolling up like a scroll.
The commentary's cosmic day folds the sky in the owner's hand; Revelation's sixth-seal vision has the sky recede as a scroll being rolled up.

column5: day of the Lord; heavens and elements dissolved
column6: The commentary names the day an arriving event that overturns the normal heavens and earth; 2 Peter's day of the Lord comes unexpectedly and dissolves the cosmic order while exposing earthly works.

column5: moon and sun ashamed when YHWH reigns
column6: The commentary binds the undoing of solar measure to the owner's unshared rule; Isaiah makes moon and sun pale before YHWH's royal reign on Zion.

column5: source dîn; Hebrew dîn; judgment after Egypt
column6: The commentary connects dîn as recompense with God's days of rescue from Pharaoh; in the promise to Abram, Hebrew dîn names God's judgment of the enslaving nation before its victims leave.
The commentary calls a remembered divine day both rescue and judgment, using Moses' deliverance as its model; Exodus explicitly marks the sea deliverance from Pharaoh as the day YHWH saved Israel.
The commentary's praise continues into the day that establishes sole rule; Israel's song after Pharaoh's defeat acclaims YHWH's kingship forever.

column5: praise after true and just judgments
column6: The commentary hears praise of the Lord of all worlds after judgment has been completed; Revelation's heavenly multitude praises God because his judgments are true and just after Babylon's fall.
The commentary pictures angels encircling the throne in praise; Revelation explicitly sets angels around the throne, elders, and living creatures as they fall and worship.

column5: YHWH goes ahead to lead on the way
column6: The commentary's owner is also the one who walks in front and gives the route; Exodus portrays YHWH going before Israel in cloud and fire to lead the way.
The commentary's flock image makes the leader's direction decisive; Jesus' shepherd goes out ahead, and the sheep follow because they know his voice.
The commentary joins herd imagery to the day on which direction and destination are disclosed; Matthew gathers all nations before the enthroned judge for a shepherd's separation of sheep from goats.

column5: all pass before him like sheep
column6: The commentary's day combines flock, an owner, and universal standing to account; the Mishnah says all inhabitants of the world pass before God like a flock on Rosh Hashanah.

column5: Lamb shepherds to springs of life-water
column6: The commentary contrasts a true leader's water with those driven toward fire and denied water; Revelation's Lamb becomes shepherd and leads the thirsty saved to springs of living water.

column5: water from rock for wilderness people
column6: The commentary calls water the thing by which a traveler can keep going; in Israel's wilderness journey, God provides water from the rock for the people at their stopping place.

column5: water begged for amid postmortem fire
column6: The commentary's condemned ask the blessed for water and cannot obtain it; the rich man in Hades asks for a drop of water to cool his tongue while in tormenting fire.

column5: debt release and the poor person's claim
column6: The commentary links a debtor's due date with the poor person's real claim on wealth; Deuteronomy forbids withholding from a poor kin because the remission year is near and treats that refusal as guilt.

column5: generosity to poor as loan repaid by YHWH
column6: The commentary imagines the day owner as a creditor who can forgive and repay; Proverbs calls generosity to the poor a loan to YHWH, who repays the giver.

column5: king begins to settle servants' accounts
column6: The commentary's dîn is a sovereign's final settlement of deferred debt; Jesus' parable opens with a king who wishes to settle accounts with his servants.
The commentary makes forgiving a debtor an earthly image of hoping for divine forgiveness; the king rebukes his servant for refusing the mercy he himself had received.
The commentary refuses to separate the just account from the merciful owner; James makes lack of mercy meet merciless judgment while saying mercy triumphs over judgment.
The commentary argues that relinquishing another's debt belongs with hope for one's own forgiveness; this talmudic maxim says that Heaven overlooks the transgressions of one who overlooks injuries.

The commentary treats forgiving a hard-pressed debtor as an image of the merciful day owner; Jesus commands lending without hope of return and connects its reward with resemblance to the merciful Father.

column5: care for the least as judgment criterion
column6: The commentary says denial of the poor's share accompanies denial of the day of recompense; the judge in Matthew identifies concrete care for the least with service rendered to himself.

column5: YHWH judges people and has compassion on servants
column6: The commentary places Rahman's mercy immediately beside his ownership of the day; Deuteronomy holds judgment and compassion together when YHWH judges his people and has compassion on his servants.

column5: no intercessor; God's own arm acts
column6: The commentary says no human can possess aid or speech on another's behalf unless the owner permits it; Isaiah sees that there is no intercessor and portrays God's own arm as bringing salvation.

The commentary allows intercession only as a prerogative of the day's owner; Hebrews gives the Christian account a continuing named intercessor, Christ, who appears to save those approaching God through him.
The commentary says even the right to speak falls under the owner on that day; Paul depicts every mouth stopped so that the whole world becomes accountable to God.

column5: account for every idle word on judgment day
column6: The commentary extends final accounting beyond outward property to words and hidden responsibility; Jesus says people will render an account for every careless word on the day of judgment.
The commentary's day has an unbending scale that judges even rulers who claim possession; Daniel's royal verdict says Belshazzar has been weighed in balances and found lacking.

column5: wealth testifies in the last days
column6: The commentary lets the hand's accumulated wealth become evidence against its owner; James says corroded gold and silver will testify against the rich and consume them like fire in the last days.

The commentary makes the merciful name immediately govern the day of judgment and leaves room for forgiveness; 4 Ezra depicts the judgment seat as the point where compassion and patience withdraw and uncompromised recompense remains.

column5: books, weighing, and adjudication of souls
column6: The commentary's book, exact reckoning, and balance form one final-account scene; the Testament of Abraham gives those elements a visionary judicial tableau in which souls are weighed and their deeds examined.

The commentary's arriving day begins with trumpet and overturns ordinary life; the Didache's closing apocalypse likewise names the trumpet and resurrection among the signs before the Lord's appearing.
The commentary's guide and path images culminate in a destination revealed at the day; the Didache opens by setting a way of life beside a way of death.

column5: way without turning right or left
column6: The commentary develops the road's middle as the route that must not be abandoned; Deuteronomy makes not turning right or left the concrete form of walking in the commanded way.
The commentary turns the owner's firm grasp into earth held and sky folded on the final day; Isaiah's creation hymn measures waters in God's hand and the heavens by his span.

column5: built objects cry out against injustice
column6: The commentary gives the final account witnesses beyond a person's self, including what hands have done; Habakkuk makes a stone from an unjust house cry out and its timber answer it.
The commentary's day removes ungranted speech before sovereign authority; Jesus' royal wedding parable renders the improperly clothed guest speechless when the king questions him.

column5: marriage of the Lamb after judgment praise
column6: The commentary uses marriage as one human binding that cannot secure a person on the day; Revelation follows its judgment praise with an eschatological marriage in which the bride is made ready for the Lamb.

column5: silence in heaven before trumpet judgments
column6: The commentary's scene of unowned speech includes silence before the day owner's action; Revelation places a half-hour of heavenly silence immediately before the trumpet judgments begin.

column5: all flesh silent before YHWH rises
column6: The commentary says speech and intercession are not human possessions in the day; Zechariah commands all flesh to be silent before YHWH as he rises from his holy dwelling.

column5: treasured possession; mercy on the day
column6: The commentary calls the day owner both merciful and the one to whom all finally belong; Malachi says that on the day he acts, YHWH will make those who fear him his treasured possession and spare them as a father spares a serving son.

column5: Day of YHWH; wrath against sinners
column6: The commentary calls the day an arriving event rather than a calendar date; Isaiah announces the coming Day of YHWH as a day of wrath that makes the land desolate and destroys its sinners.

column5: source yawm; Hebrew yom; approaching bitter day
column6: The commentary gives yawm the force of an approaching overwhelming event; cognate Hebrew yom in Zephaniah's Day of YHWH is near, bitter, and marked by the warrior's cry rather than ordinary solar routine.
The commentary's day makes those who have died arrive for final accounting; Isaiah speaks of the dead living, corpses rising, and those in the dust awakening.
The commentary makes leading a flock a form of responsible possession; Ezekiel has God oppose the self-feeding shepherds, require his sheep from their hand, and reclaim the flock.

column5: judgment between sheep, rams, and goats
column6: The commentary turns flock imagery into a day of differentiation and account; Ezekiel explicitly says God judges between sheep and sheep, rams and goats.
The commentary contrasts the true caller who leads straight with Pharaoh's fatal leadership; Isaiah says a people's leaders make them err and those led by them are swallowed up.

column5: YHWH at the head of a people going out
column6: The commentary's guide is the one who goes before and determines the route; Micah's restoration procession has its king pass before the people with YHWH at their head.
The commentary's false front-runner brings followers to fire instead of water; Jesus calls false leaders blind guides and says guide and follower alike fall into a pit.

column5: hour of judgment; worship of Creator
column6: The commentary joins sole ownership, the coming day, and worship; Revelation's angel announces that the hour of God's judgment has come and calls all to worship the maker of heaven, earth, sea, and springs.

column5: coming with recompense for each work
column6: The commentary defines dîn as exact return for what each person has done; the coming speaker in Revelation brings recompense to repay each according to work.

column5: repayment to each according to works
column6: The commentary makes final repayment individual and proportionate; Paul states the same judicial rule in saying that God renders to each person according to works.

column5: all exposed before the one to whom account is due
column6: The commentary says the hidden interior reaches the account after human witnesses stop; Hebrews says no creature is hidden and all are naked and exposed before the one to whom account must be given.
The commentary uses the deathbed to show that a person cannot recover the life already claimed; Hebrews sets death once for humans and judgment afterward.

column5: bring nothing in; take nothing out
column6: The commentary says possessions, servants, and status are left behind when the person comes alone; Paul states the compact formula that nothing was brought into the world and nothing can be taken out.

The commentary moves from naming the owner to direct address and treats debt forgiveness as the measure of hoped-for mercy; the Lord's Prayer asks the Father to forgive debts as petitioners forgive their debtors.

column5: postmortem reversal of comfort and anguish
column6: The commentary's denied water scene is a recompense in which prior possession no longer helps; Abraham explains the rich man's torment and Lazarus's comfort as a reversal of their former received portions.

column5: withheld wages cry to the Lord
column6: The commentary binds denial of the poor's due to the day of account; James says unpaid wages cry out and the cries of harvesters reach the Lord of hosts.

column5: Christ titled King of kings and Lord of lords
column6: The commentary concentrates final kingship in the one divine owner of the day; Revelation gives the victorious Christ the title King of kings and Lord of lords, a specifically Christian royal identification.
The commentary links debt's due date to ownership and servitude; Proverbs states the social analogy directly by making the borrower servant to the lender.

column5: God weighs heart and repays work
column6: The commentary's unbending scale reaches the heart as well as outward deeds; Proverbs asks whether the one who weighs the heart does not know and then says he repays each according to work.
The commentary turns the day into a balance that cannot bend for wealth or status; Job asks to be weighed in just scales so that God may know his integrity.
The commentary describes the day as an event that arrives with fire and judgment; Isaiah presents YHWH entering judgment with fire and sword against all flesh.

column5: Lord Jesus revealed in flaming fire
column6: The commentary names the single owner as the judge of the fire-bound day; 2 Thessalonians presents the revealed Lord Jesus in flaming fire as the one inflicting retribution, a Christian specification of the judging figure.

The commentary treats death, return, and accounting as one continuous claim of the day owner; Avot's maxim makes those born die, the dead live, and the living stand for judgment before the King of kings.

The commentary uses debt writing and commercial honesty to show that ordinary accounts continue before God; this talmudic judgment scene begins by asking whether a person conducted business faithfully.

column5: one mediator between God and humans
column6: The commentary limits effective intercession to the owner's authorization; 1 Timothy states a Christian mediatorial formula that names one God and one mediator, the human Christ Jesus.

column5: throne before which earth and sky flee
column6: The commentary's day has the earth grasped and the heavens folded beneath sovereign rule; at Revelation's great white throne, earth and sky flee from the judge's presence.

The commentary uses spouse and family bonds to show relations that cannot carry another person through the day; Jesus recasts the resurrection state as one in which people neither marry nor are given in marriage.
The commentary calls the owned day the time when all accounts close; Qohelet says God judges righteous and wicked because there is a time for every matter and every work.
The commentary describes dîn as a counterweight that returns what a person has done; Jesus says the measure used for others will be measured back to the user.
The commentary sees final recompense as the completion of habitual conduct rather than an isolated act; Paul says no one mocks God because whatever a person sows, that he will also reap.
